title: The protein sweet spot for muscle is about 1.6 g per kg
snippet: A meta-analysis of 49 trials found extra protein boosts strength-training gains, up to about 1.6 g per kg a day.
bullets: 49 studies, 1,863 participants.[1]
Protein boosted gains in strength, fat-free mass and muscle size during resistance training.[1]
Beyond about 1.62 g/kg/day, there was no further gain.[1]

report.t: Protein supplements significantly increased strength and muscle gains in trials of 6+ weeks of resistance training.[1]
Above ~1.62 g of protein per kg per day, extra protein didn't add more fat-free mass.[1]
The benefit shrank with age and was bigger in people who already trained.[1]

Spread protein across meals: eggs or Greek yoghurt at breakfast, a palm-sized portion of meat, fish or tofu at lunch and dinner. Above about 1.62 g per kg a day, extra protein added no more muscle in the review.[1] Lifting is the signal; protein is the material.

why: For a more muscular look, training plus enough protein is the proven base. No magic peptides needed.
tryit: Multiply your weight in kg by 1.6, then check one day of eating against that number.
qa: How much protein do I need for muscle?
Gains plateaued above about 1.62 g per kg of body weight per day.[1]
Does protein work without training?
This research looked at protein alongside resistance training.[1]
Does age matter?
Yes. The benefit got smaller with age.[1]
How big was the study?
49 trials and 1,863 participants.[1]

Eligible people can be offered gonorrhoea, mpox, hepatitis A and B, and HPV vaccines.[1]

A medicine that reduces the risk of getting HIV.[3]

No. Clinic staff will check what's right for you.

title: Hyperfocus: the ADHD 'zone' scientists are now measuring
snippet: Adults with more ADHD symptoms report more hyperfocus: long stretches of intense, absorbed attention.
bullets: Hupfeld et al. built an Adult Hyperfocus Questionnaire and tested two samples, 251 and 372 adults.[1]
More ADHD symptoms went with more hyperfocus.[1]
Hyperfocus is intense concentration that locks onto one subject or task.[2]

report.t: Adults with ADHD often report long, highly focused attention, even though they're easily distracted.[1]
A preregistered study of 251 and 372 adults found hyperfocus was more common with higher ADHD symptoms.[1]
Hyperfocus is intense concentration on one subject or task.[2] The trick is choosing what gets it before it chooses for you.

Pick one high-value task. Remove other tabs. Put water and a snack nearby. Set an alarm for 90 minutes as a stop cue. Hyperfocus is intense absorption in one task,[2] and the study shows it's a real, common ADHD experience,[1] so plan for it.

why: Your attention isn't broken. It runs on interest, so feed it the right fuel.
tryit: Before deep work, set a timer and a 'stop cue' (alarm + glass of water) so hyperfocus doesn't eat your day.
qa: What is hyperfocus?
Intense concentration on one subject or task.[2]
Is hyperfocus linked to ADHD?
Yes. More ADHD symptoms went with more hyperfocus in two adult samples.[1]
How was it measured?
With the new Adult Hyperfocus Questionnaire, in 251 and 372 adults.[1]
How can I use it well?
Pick the task first, set an end cue and protect the time. That's practical advice, not a study finding.

title: The 'if-then' trick that turns intentions into action
snippet: Implementation intentions ('If it's 8am, then I open the report') are a well-studied way to close the gap between meaning to and doing.
bullets: An implementation intention is a self-regulation strategy in an if-then format.[1]
A 2006 meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran reviewed its effects on reaching goals.[1]
It's also been studied for shielding goals from unwanted thoughts and feelings.[1]

report.h: Goals are vague, cues are sharp
report.t: 'Exercise more' floats. 'If I finish my coffee, then I put on trainers' fires.[1]
Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 meta-analysis pulled together the evidence on if-then plans and goal achievement.[1]
Tying an action to a cue means you don't have to rely on remembering it.

'If I open my laptop, then I write one line of the proposal.' 'If I feel the urge to scroll, then I take three breaths first.' 'If it's Sunday at 6pm, then I plan Monday's top task.' If-then plans link a cue to an action.[1]

why: It hands the remembering to your surroundings, which is ideal for ADHD.
tryit: Write one: 'If [time or place], then I will [tiny action].' Put it on your lock screen.
qa: What is an implementation intention?
An if-then plan that links a situation to a goal-directed action.[1]
Is there evidence?
Yes. A 2006 meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran reviewed its effects.[1]
Can it help with negative thoughts?
It's been studied for shielding goals from unwanted thoughts and feelings.[1]
Give me an example
'If I sit at my desk at 9, then I open the one task I picked last night.'

title: Self-compassion has 3 parts, and you can train each one
snippet: Psychologist Kristin Neff defines self-compassion as self-kindness, common humanity and mindfulness.
bullets: Self-compassion means extending compassion to yourself when you fail or suffer.[1]
Neff's 3 parts: self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness.[1]
Her site offers free guided exercises.[2]

report.t: Self-kindness means being warm with yourself when you hit pain or shortcomings, instead of harsh.[1]
Common humanity: struggle is part of being human, not proof you're broken.[1]
Mindfulness means seeing the pain clearly without blowing it up.[1] Neff's free exercises make it practical.[2]

When you mess up, notice the critic's voice. Then run the three parts: name it (mindfulness), remember everyone struggles (common humanity), and speak kindly (self-kindness).[1] Neff's site has free guided practices if you'd like to be walked through it.[2]

why: Turning the inner critic into an inner coach is a skill, not a personality trait.
tryit: Next time you mess up, ask: 'What would I say to a friend right now?' Then say it to yourself.
qa: What is self-compassion?
Extending compassion to yourself in moments of inadequacy, failure or suffering.[1]
What are the three parts?
Self-kindness, common humanity and mindfulness, as defined by Kristin Neff.[1]
Is it the same as self-esteem?
No. Self-compassion is about how you treat yourself when things go wrong.[1]
Where can I practise?
Kristin Neff's site has free guided practices and exercises.[2]

title: The 3-sentence 'self-compassion break' for hard moments
snippet: Kristin Neff's exercise: name the suffering, remember everyone struggles, and offer yourself kindness.
bullets: Bring a stressful situation to mind and notice it in your body.[1]
Say: 'This is a moment of suffering.'[1]
Then: 'May I be kind to myself,' or find the phrase you need to hear.[1]

report.t: 'This is a moment of suffering.' That's mindfulness in one sentence.[1]
Remind yourself that suffering is part of life. It's the common-humanity step.[1]
Hand on chest if it helps, then 'May I be kind to myself.' Or ask, 'What do I need to hear right now?'[1]

After a tough meeting, a rejection or a mistake. You can do it silently on a train or in a bathroom. If the words feel stiff, the exercise invites you to find your own phrase, the thing you most need to hear right now.[1]

why: It takes 60 seconds and interrupts the spiral of harsh self-talk.
tryit: Try it once today, even on something small. Notice what changes in your body.
qa: What do I say?
'This is a moment of suffering,' then a reminder that suffering is part of life, then 'May I be kind to myself.'[1]
Why the hand on the chest?
The exercise suggests soothing touch, like feeling the warmth of your hands on your chest.[1]
What if the words feel fake?
Ask what you need to hear right now and use your own phrase.[1]
Who created it?
Kristin Neff, a leading self-compassion researcher.[1]

title: Talk to yourself by name. It calms nerves
snippet: Using your own name instead of 'I' under stress helped people perform better and worry less, across 7 studies.
bullets: 7 studies, 585 people (Kross et al., 2014).[1]
Using your name or 'you' instead of 'I' created more psychological distance.[1]
Those people did better at first impressions and public speaking, with less distress.[1]

report.t: 'Why is Junior nervous?' instead of 'Why am I nervous?' That small switch creates distance.[1]
In first-impression and public-speaking tests, the non-'I' group did better according to objective raters.[1]
They also felt less distress and dwelt on it less afterwards.[1]

Before a negotiation, presentation or difficult call, take 20 seconds: 'Junior, you've prepared for this. Focus on the next step.' In the studies, this kind of self-talk improved performance and cut distress.[1] It also helped people dwell less afterwards.[1]

why: Before a pitch or tough negotiation, it's a free, instant confidence tool.
tryit: Before your next big call, say: 'Junior, you've prepared. You can do this.'
qa: What did Kross find?
Using your own name or non-first-person pronouns under stress improved performance and reduced distress.[1]
How many people?
585 people across 7 studies.[1]
Does it help with public speaking?
Yes. The non-first-person group performed better and felt less distress.[1]
Isn't it weird?
Maybe, but you can do it silently.

title: 15 minutes of honest writing, 4 days in a row
snippet: Psychologist James Pennebaker's 'expressive writing' asks you to put your deepest thoughts about something hard on paper.
bullets: Expressive writing was developed by James W. Pennebaker in the late 1980s.[1]
In the first study, people wrote their deepest thoughts and feelings about a past trauma.[1]
They wrote non-stop for 15 minutes a day, 4 days in a row.[1]

report.t: Write about something difficult, your deepest thoughts and feelings, with no editing.[1]
15 minutes a day for 4 days in a row. Keep writing even if you repeat yourself.[1]
Private, messy, and you can throw it away. The point is processing, not prose.

Pick a quiet time, set a 15-minute timer, and write without stopping. Spelling doesn't matter. In the classic method, participants wrote on 4 consecutive days.[1] It's normal to feel a bit stirred up at first. Stop if it feels like too much.

why: Racing thoughts get quieter once they're on paper.
tryit: Tonight, set a 15-minute timer and write about what's weighing on you. Then delete or shred it.
qa: What is expressive writing?
A method developed by James Pennebaker: write your deepest thoughts and feelings about a difficult experience.[1]
How long do I write?
15 minutes a day for 4 days in a row, as in the classic study.[1]
What if I run out of things to say?
Participants were told to go back to the beginning and repeat or rephrase.[1]
Do I need to share it?
No. It's private.

title: AI made support agents 14% faster, and beginners 34% faster
snippet: A study of 5,179 customer support agents found an AI assistant raised the number of issues resolved per hour.

Productivity rose 14% on average.[1]
Novice and low-skilled workers improved 34%. Experienced experts barely changed.[1]

report.t: Not a lab demo: it tracked thousands of agents using an AI assistant on the job.[1]
Newer workers gained most, 34%, as the AI spread the habits of top performers.[1]
AI is a fast way to perform closer to expert level in areas you're new to, like a new business or market.

report.h: Use AI like a senior colleague

why: Learning deal-making? AI can be an on-demand coach while you build the skill.

A 14% average rise in issues resolved per hour, and 34% for novices.[1]
Who benefited least?
Experienced, highly skilled workers saw minimal impact.[1]
Why do beginners gain most?
The authors suggest the AI spreads the best practices of more able workers.[1]
How many workers were studied?
5,179 customer support agents.[1]

Hardware costs fell about 30% a year and energy efficiency improved 40% a year.[1]
Open-weight models are closing the gap with closed ones.[1]

report.t: What cost dollars now costs cents. Stanford HAI tracked a 280-fold drop.[1]
Capable small models, hardware getting about 30% cheaper a year, and 40% better energy efficiency.[1]
When a tool gets this much cheaper, new uses open up: personal agents, bots and automations that used to cost too much.

When a key cost drops this much, look for tasks you skipped because they were too expensive or slow: summarising documents, drafting proposals, monitoring prices or news. The AI Index shows costs falling fast.[1] Small businesses can now afford tools that were enterprise-only.

Over 280× cheaper for GPT-3.5-level performance, Nov 2022 to Oct 2024.[1]

More capable small models, hardware costs falling about 30% a year and efficiency up about 40% a year.[1]

Stanford HAI, in its 2025 AI Index Report.[1]

Models whose weights are released publicly. They're closing the gap with closed models.[1]

12 October 2025, fully operational from 10 April 2026.[1]

bullets: The remittance basis ended on 6 April 2025.[1]

Claiming means losing your tax-free personal allowance and CGT allowance.[1]

report.h: Domicile is out, residence is in
report.t: UK tax now hinges on tax residence under the Statutory Residence Test, not domicile.[2]
If you become UK resident after 10 years of non-residence, you can claim relief on eligible foreign income and gains for up to 4 tax years.[1]
Claiming costs your personal allowance and CGT annual exemption, and you claim on your Self Assessment return.[1]

report.h: Questions to ask a tax adviser
report.t: Am I UK tax resident under the Statutory Residence Test? Do I qualify for the 4-year FIG regime? Is claiming worth losing my personal allowance?[1] Residence-based rules replaced domicile from 6 April 2025,[2] so old non-dom advice may be out of date.

UK tax residents in their first 4 years after at least 10 years of non-UK residence.[1]

On your Self Assessment tax return.[1]

title: Your accent isn't the problem. Clarity is
snippet: In a classic study, how strong an accent was didn't slow listeners down. Hard-to-understand speech did.
bullets: Munro & Derwing (1995): 20 native listeners judged true/false sentences from native and accented speakers.[1]
Speech rated hard to understand took longer to process.[1]
But the strength of the accent wasn't linked to processing time.[1]

report.t: Listeners weren't slowed down by how strong the accent was.[1]
What slowed listeners was speech rated hard to understand.[1]
Work on the sounds and stress that cause misunderstandings, not on erasing where you're from.

why: Your Brazilian accent is part of you. Clarity is what changes how you're heard.

title: Shadowing: repeat native speech a split second behind
snippet: Speech shadowing, repeating what you hear with a tiny delay, is a lab technique that's also used for language learning.
bullets: Speech shadowing means repeating speech with a short delay after you hear it.[1]
The delay reflects how long the brain takes to process and respond.[1]
It's used in language learning, interpreting and singing.[1]

report.t: Play audio and speak along a beat behind, copying the rhythm and melody.[1]
It trains listening and speaking at once, which is why it's used in language learning and interpreting.[1]
No textbook needed. Just a podcast you love and 5 minutes.

1. Listen to a 30-second clip once. 2. Play it again and speak along a beat behind. 3. Repeat three times, then record yourself. Shadowing is a recognised technique in language learning and interpreting.[1] Pick speakers whose style you'd like to sound like.

why: It builds the music of English, its rhythm and stress, which shapes how natural you sound.
tryit: Pick a 1-minute clip from a podcast you like and shadow it 3 times today.
qa: What is shadowing?
Repeating speech with a short delay after hearing it.[1]
Is it used for language learning?
Yes, along with interpreting and singing.[1]
How long should I practise?
Start with 5 minutes a day so it's easy to stick with.
What should I shadow?
Clear speech you enjoy, like a favourite podcast host.

title: Learn words right before you forget them
snippet: Spaced repetition brings words back at growing intervals. It's ideal for vocabulary.
bullets: Spaced repetition schedules reviews at growing intervals to beat the forgetting curve.[1]

report.t: Review just as a memory starts to fade, and each review lasts longer.[1]

report.t: Apps like Anki schedule your reviews automatically.[1]

why: Phrasal verbs and idioms stick when an app brings them back at the right moment.

Reviewing material at increasing intervals to beat the forgetting curve.[1]
